Paper.Title: Into the Storm: Engineering an Accelerated Graduate Curriculum to Create Military Weather Officers
Paper.Abstract: The Air Force's Basic Meteorology Program (BMP) at the Air Force Institute of Technology (AFIT) rapidly transforms newly-commissioned STEM undergraduates from other disciplines into defense-minded atmospheric scientists. Adopted by AFIT in 2024 and elevated to a one-year graduate certificate, the program was re-built from the ground up by its faculty. As part of this effort, I was brought on to design and lead five of the program's nine core meteorology courses. These courses are a fusion of modern pedagogy, AI-enhanced lectures, and challenging projects that propel students into the world of atmospheric science and military operations. From designing and fielding their own environmental sensors to advising the Wright-Brothers or Allied Command Headquarters in time-travel assisted forecast labs, this innovative curriculum ensures its officers are prepared to meet the complex weather and environmental Science needs of the defense community, anytime and anywhere. This presentation will share experiences from bringing this blank-slate program online, as well as key components from its exciting curriculum.

Paper.Title: Teaching Wave-Mean Flow Interaction Via Active Learning
Paper.Abstract: The interaction of atmospheric waves with the background flow is an essential topic in advanced atmospheric dynamics courses, but usually at the graduate level. Phenomena ranging from the quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO) in the tropical stratosphere to sudden stratospheric warmings in the polar stratosphere are inexplicable and unpredictable without an understanding of wave-mean flow interaction. Conversely, tropospheric phenomena such as convection and flow over mountains have a large impact on the climatology of every layer of the atmosphere via wave-mean flow interaction, which broadens our perspective on the interconnectedness of tropospheric weather and global climate. The mathematical concepts of wave-mean flow interaction are advanced and at the outer limit of what undergraduates can understand; however, the basic physical concepts of wave breaking and "surf zones" are familiar to anyone who has spent time on a beach. McIntyre and Norton (1990 Journal of Fluid Mechanics, Fig. 1) illustrated a "simple lecture or laboratory demonstration" of wave-mean flow interaction using an oscillating wavemaker, water, and some visible tracer. For the past 22 years I have incorporated this demonstration in my undergraduate Geophysical Fluid Dynamics and Atmospheric Dynamics II classes at the University of Georgia. This demonstration is used as the motivator for discussion of advanced dynamical topics such as Stokes drift, the transformed Euler mean equations, the Eliassen-Palm flux divergence, Rossby wave breaking, sudden stratospheric warmings, gravity wave breaking, and the QBO. While these concepts are included in chapters 10 and 12 of Holton and Hakim's canonical text, they are rarely, if ever, broached at the undergraduate level, according to the survey of Klees et al. (2025 Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society). In this presentation I will present video and photos of the classroom demonstration; discuss student reactions to this demonstration; and encourage other atmospheric dynamics instructors to consider incorporating this active learning approach to wave-mean flow interaction in the graduate and (even) the undergraduate dynamics curriculum.

Paper.Title: Two Stage Exams for Assessing Learning and Enhancing Student Engagement in an Upper-level Meteorology Course
Paper.Abstract:
A two-stage exam is a relatively simple way to assess learning while also encouraging collaborative learning and retention of information. In a two-stage exam, students first complete and turn in the exam individually, and then, working in small groups, answer similar exam questions again. Two-stage exams are not new, but they are relatively rare in meteorology courses. In my prior iterations of teaching Dynamic Meteorology I and II at Virginia Tech, students have expressed some dissatisfaction with the lack of follow-up on exams about the questions they may have missed. Furthermore, students struggle with retaining knowledge about some concepts when they are encountered again later in the course. In the context of this class, the two-stage exam was administered over two days with one day in between to allow the students to reflect on their performance and review any concepts that they may not have understood in the first stage of the exam. During the second stage, the students collaborated and received immediate targeted feedback from their peers within their assigned group and their instructor. For context, the two-stage exam was used for the two midterm exams, and the final exam was a take-home exam. To evaluate the effectiveness of this new exam approach, a survey was administered on the last day of class.

In this study, the population was undergraduate students in my Dynamic Meteorology II course. These students were meteorology majors in their junior or senior year and had taken Dynamic Meteorology I (with traditional exams) in the previous fall semester. Students were incentivized to participate in the survey with one extra-credit percentage points toward their final course grade. The questionnaire was designed as a pencil-and-paper instrument that was administered to all students who attended the last day of class during the spring 2025 semester. The questionnaire asked each student to answer a series of closed-response questions that included their year of study (i.e., freshman, sophomore, junior, senior), their gender, their prior experience with two-stage exams, and their level of agreement (i.e., 5=strongly agree, 4=agree, 3=neutral, 2=disagree, 1=strongly disagree) with 10 statements that were designed to measure the extent to which the two stage exam influenced several domains of engagement and satisfaction with their learning experience. The 10 statements were based on (i) the potential benefits of two stage exams, as outlined by the literature, and (ii) an attempt to measure the emotional, cognitive, and behavioral effects of the two-stage exam on student engagement. In addition to closed-response questions, the survey also asked each student to describe, in open-response format, what they liked "most" and what they liked "least" about their experience with the two-stage exam strategy.

The end of the semester survey results suggest that students were generally positive about the two-stage exam, with the vast majority of students indicating that they preferred the two-stage exam to the more traditional exam that was administered in the first semester of the class. More specifically, the students reported that the two stage-exam strategy led to improved confidence, improved collaboration skills, enhanced critical thinking skills, and an improved grade compared with a traditional exam. Results were more mixed for whether the two-stage exam was “more enjoyable” or “reduced anxiety.” Open ended feedback included generally positive remarks about the two-stage exam, except for some comments about the length of the exam (two days spread over a week), which led to more stress for some students. Based on these results, I plan to continue using the two-stage exam with some minor changes to reduce student anxiety about the new exam strategy.

Paper.Title: Bringing the Stratosphere to Statistics
Paper.Abstract: Activities and assignments in most statistics courses need contexts: real data to analyze and real questions to answer. It has become relatively common for statistics courses to use datasets related to severe storms or temperature and carbon dioxide trends, but other connections to atmospheric science are much more rare. However, students are often curious about weather and climate, so these courses provide an opportunity to expose a wide audience to a broader range of atmospheric science topics. The author introduced data and questions related to stratospheric dynamics and chemistry across undergraduate statistics courses for students from a wide variety of disciplines. Particular examples discussed will include comparing stratospheric dynamics in El Niño and La Niña winters in introductory statistics courses, modeling sudden stratospheric warming frequency in a probability theory course, and using a paper on stratospheric aerosol injection as a model of statistical communication in an advanced statistics course. The presentation will share reflections on these assignments and activities from the instructor and student perspectives as well as considerations for future inclusion of atmospheric science topics in courses in other disciplines.

Paper.Title: Weathergami and Climate Characterization
Paper.Abstract: The weathergami chart, a bivariate heat map showing the occurrence frequencies of all combinations of daily maximum and minimum temperatures observed at a particular location, is an engaging weather visualization that can be utilized to characterize local climates. Local climate is traditionally characterized using the climograph, a chart depicting the annual progression of average monthly temperature and precipitation. Weathergami charts illustrate the variability and extremes in daily temperature and daily temperature range, and thus provide an attractive supplement to the climograph for characterizing the diverse range of climates found on earth.

Paper.Title: Influence of Tropical Cyclones on the Diurnal Cycle of Lightning over the Mexican Continental Territory
Paper.Abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) over the Eastern Pacific Ocean and Gulf of Mexico influence the convective activity over the Mexican continental territory (MCT). The increased convection can lead to lightning production. Besides, the MCT is characterized by the presence of diurnal cycles of lightning. However, it is not well known how diurnal cycles of lightning over the MCT are influenced by the occurrence of TCs. Two case studies of TCs that occurred in 2018 and 2021, over the Eastern Pacific Ocean and Gulf of Mexico, were selected to evaluate their effect on the observed diurnal variability of lightning over the Mexican continental territory. The systems were simulated with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and compared with lightning observations. Different sea surface temperatures (SSTs) were used as the button boundary of the model to conduct the different simulations (with different model configurations) for the two selected cases. The diurnal variability of lightning calculated from the simulations shows a dependence of both the SST and the TCs. The transport of moisture from the ocean to the continental region plays an important role. In additional semi-idealized experiments, the diurnal variability of lightning shows changes in amplitude when the SST is cooled or heated. Because lightning is associated with strong convection, it can be important to understand how an occurring TC influences the diurnal variability of lightning, which shows a strong diurnal cycle, over the MCT.
